source.title: NeuronMotif: Deciphering cis-regulatory codes by layer-wise demixing of deep neural networks
source.authors: Zheng Wei; Kui Hua; Lei Wei; Shining Ma; Rui Jiang; Xuegong Zhang; Yanda Li; Wing Hong Wong; Xiao-Wo Wang

record.file_problem: The full text is present. It is headed as a bioRxiv preprint, while the supplied metadata identifies the PNAS publication.
record.tranche_reason: Applies neuron-level motif interpretation to genomic-sequence convolutional networks and reports results relevant to neuron interpretability, but does not test any listed version in its specified models or setting.
record.gate_note: The study analyzes convolutional neurons in DNA-sequence models, not language-model neuron poles or the listed Inception/large-language-model cases. It does not estimate the share of neurons with one or multiple jobs or test explanations on held-out activating inputs. Results about motif mixtures and architecture are recorded as findings about the broader subject, under versions ["none"]. Comparisons of interpretation methods and cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study builds NeuronMotif to decouple motif mixtures in convolutional neurons of DNA-sequence CNNs (Basset, DeepSEA, and in-house BD-5, BD-10, DD-10). It reports no share of neurons with one or several jobs, no language or vision models, and no tests of explanations against held-out activations. Its closest finding is to V4's idea that mixed neurons come from architecture or regularization and weak tools. That finding is qualitative, in a different kind of system, and reports no interpretable-neuron share, so no version is tested. It is recorded under fits_no_version. The relation is set to 'discusses' only as the nearest available option: the paper neither cites nor uses the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors model each neuron as a latent-variable mixture, split into shift mixtures from max-pooling and synonymous-motif mixtures. They treat synonymous mixtures as adversarial-noise-like defects, not signal. Deeper small-kernel models (BD-10, DD-10) reduce these defects and predict better (higher AUPRC).
record.recipe_differences: Uses a sampling and K-means-based procedure to infer DNA sequence motifs and motif combinations in convolutional networks; it is not an audit of language-model neuron explanations or a held-out activation-prediction evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that synonymous-motif problems vary with architecture and regularization: larger kernels and pooling can weaken coupling, while their deeper, smaller-kernel/pooling models suppress the problem. DeepSEA regularization suppresses noise but is associated with dead neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: In Basset, apparent mixtures in L2 and L3 neurons come partly from max-pooling shifts. NeuronMotif splits these into 3 or 12 consistent shifted motifs, where older max-activation and saliency tools gave noisy, low-information motifs. A better tool turns apparently mixed neurons into coherent ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In genomic CNNs, much apparent neuron mixing is shift diversity from max-pooling that a structure-aware decoupling tool resolves into one consistent motif.

fits_no_version.finding: Synonymous-motif mixing is common in Basset L3 but rare in L2. It is suppressed in deeper, smaller-kernel models (BD-10, DD-10) and by strong regularization in DeepSEA, the latter at the cost of dead units (150 in L2 and 120 in L3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In genomic CNNs, the degree of neuron mixing depends on architecture and regularization, with deeper small-kernel models showing fewer mixed and dead units.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
record.problems: The reported neuron-mixture diagnostics are largely qualitative in the text and do not provide a proportion of neurons with interpretable versus mixed functions. NeuronMotif sampling is used to characterize the models; the study does not test explanations on held-out activating inputs as in V6 or V7.
record.rows_left_out: Interpretation-method comparisons and motif-matching performance in Figs. 3 and 5 were not recorded because they compare the authors' method with other methods rather than quantify a listed claim outcome. Prediction-performance comparisons were not recorded because AUPRC is not a measure of neuron interpretability. Cited literature results were excluded.

untested.parts: All of it: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit shares.
All of it: other language models, dense and MoE, and scale.
All of it: InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization versus superposition.
Share of interpretable neurons in vision models and how it rises with tools or architecture. Only a qualitative genomic-CNN analogue is reported.
All of it: neuron-based attribution graphs versus replacement models.
All of it: whether explanations from activating examples predict firing.
All of it: simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Genomic CNN interpretability paper with no connection to the essay or to the OpenAI neuron-explanation work. The reader's 'tests'/T3 is downgraded: no version names this kind of system or measure, and no neuron-share statistic is reported. The text is the bioRxiv preprint; the metadata is the PNAS version.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B pole audit and its one-job, two-job, and not-understood shares.
Language-model comparisons, dense versus mixture-of-experts models, and scaling up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose interpretation, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
The stated Inception-sized vision-model estimates and whether a share of interpretable neurons rises with tools or modern vision architectures.
Attribution graphs using a large model's own neurons and comparison with a trained replacement model and reconstruction error.
Testing explanations against where a neuron fires on activating examples not used to write the explanation.
Automated scoring of language-model neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: Basset
rows.operation_detail: Compared motif-consensus-sequence activation with the maximum activation of sampled sequences to diagnose synonymous-motif mixtures.
rows.measure: The two indicators were described as almost consistent.
rows.locator: Results, “DCNN diagnosis and architecture design guidance”; Fig. 4c
rows.note: Qualitative diagnostic result; this is not a count of neurons with a single job.

rows.subject: Basset
rows.operation_detail: Compared motif-consensus-sequence activation with the maximum activation of sampled sequences to diagnose synonymous-motif mixtures.
rows.measure: Consensus-sequence activations for many decoupled motifs were negative and severely deviated from the maximum activation values.
rows.value: Many consensus activations negative and severely deviated
rows.locator: Results, “DCNN diagnosis and architecture design guidance”; Fig. 4c
rows.note: The authors attribute most problematic motifs to combining different synonymous motifs; no population share of interpretable neurons is reported.

rows.subject: DeepSEA
rows.operation_detail: Counted convolutional neurons that were dead, meaning no sampled input activated them.
rows.locator: Results, “DCNN diagnosis and architecture design guidance”
rows.note: The text reports the count during NeuronMotif sampling.
rows.check: The value is correct, but a denominator is needed. The DeepSEA layers have 480 (L2) and 960 (L3) kernels per Methods, so 150 and 120 dead units are about 31% and 12.5%.

rows.subject: DeepSEA
rows.operation_detail: Counted convolutional neurons that were dead, meaning no sampled input activated them.
rows.locator: Results, “DCNN diagnosis and architecture design guidance”
rows.note: The text reports the count during NeuronMotif sampling.
rows.check: The denominator is 960 L3 kernels (Methods), about 12.5% dead. The link to none is correct.

rows.subject: BD-10
rows.operation_detail: Diagnosed synonymous-motif problems and dead kernels after using a deeper architecture with smaller kernels and pooling sizes.

conditions.value: 10 convolutional layers; kernel size 3 and max-pooling size 2, with first-layer kernel size set to 7

rows.measure: Severity of synonymous-motif problem and presence of dead kernels
rows.baseline: Basset model; no numeric baseline stated
rows.value: Synonymous-motif problem significantly suppressed; few dead kernels found
rows.locator: Results, “DCNN diagnosis and architecture design guidance”; Methods, “DCNN architecture optimization and deeper DCNN model construction”
rows.note: The statement is qualitative here; no fraction of interpretable neurons is supplied.
rows.check: The baseline is Basset (3 conv layers, large kernels and pooling). The comparison is shown only qualitatively in Fig. 4c.

rows.subject: DD-10
rows.operation_detail: Diagnosed synonymous-motif problems and dead kernels after using a deeper architecture with smaller kernels and pooling sizes.

conditions.value: 10 convolutional layers; kernel size 3 and max-pooling size 2, with first-layer kernel size set to 7

rows.measure: Severity of synonymous-motif problem and presence of dead kernels
rows.baseline: DeepSEA model; no numeric baseline stated
rows.value: Synonymous-motif problem significantly suppressed; few dead kernels found
rows.locator: Results, “DCNN diagnosis and architecture design guidance”; Methods, “DCNN architecture optimization and deeper DCNN model construction”
rows.note: The text also says strong regularization in DeepSEA suppresses synonymous-motif noise at the cost of dead neurons.
rows.check: The baseline is DeepSEA, which used strong regularization. DD-10 was trained without regularization (Methods). The comparison is qualitative (Fig. 4b).
